standard.title: Storylines across contexts
standard.description: recognise similar storylines, ideas and relationships in different contexts in literary texts by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss characters, events and settings across different cultural and contextual contexts in literature (AC9E3LE01). They have not yet recognised similar storylines, ideas and relationships across First Nations Australian, Australian and world literary texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify common storylines, themes and relationship patterns across literary texts from different cultural contexts — including First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors — and explain how context shapes the way these universal patterns are expressed.

nodes.label: Identifying recurring storylines
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify a recurring storyline pattern (e.g. journey, transformation, conflict and resolution) across two or more texts from different contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a similar storyline in two texts from different cultural contexts and explain what makes the storylines similar.
nodes.typical_width: Identify recurring storyline patterns — journey, transformation, rescue, coming-of-age, conflict — across at least three texts from different cultural contexts, including at least one First Nations Australian text, and explain what the patterns share.
wider: Investigate how the same universal storyline pattern (e.g. the hero's journey) appears in First Nations Australian, European and Asian literary traditions and discuss similarities and differences
Read texts by the same author and track how recurring storyline patterns or character relationships appear across their work

response_modes.reason: Recognising storyline patterns is a capability built through encountering many texts. The wider the textual repertoire, the stronger the pattern-recognition ability becomes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of cultural and literary contexts available for comparison — especially First Nations Australian literary traditions — is genuinely wide and pedagogically rich.
success_criteria: Can identify a shared storyline pattern across two texts from different cultural contexts
Can explain what makes the storylines similar despite being set in different contexts

nodes.label: Themes and connections to experience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the theme of a literary text and connect it to their own experience, other texts and the wider world.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the theme of a literary text and make one connection to personal experience, another text or a real-world issue.
nodes.typical_width: Identify themes across a range of texts from different cultural contexts, making connections between texts and between texts and the world, and explaining how themes carry meaning beyond the specific story.
wider: Compare how a theme (e.g. belonging, courage, loss) is treated differently across texts from different cultural contexts and discuss what each treatment reveals about cultural values
Explore how themes in First Nations Australian literature connect to Country, community and cultural knowledge, and consider how these themes differ from Western literary treatments of similar ideas
success_criteria: Can name the theme of a text and explain it in their own words
Can make at least one connection between the theme and their own experience or another text

nodes.label: Characters, settings and cultural context
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural context shapes the way characters, settings and relationships are portrayed in a text, even when the underlying storyline is familiar.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one way that the cultural context of a text shapes how a familiar character type or relationship is portrayed.
nodes.typical_width: Compare how characters, settings and relationships in texts from different cultural backgrounds reflect the values and contexts of their origins, while sharing underlying patterns with texts from other cultures.
wider: Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander characters and settings in First Nations Australian literature reflect cultural knowledge and relationships with Country that differ from Western literary portrayals
Research an author from a culture different from one's own and examine how their biography and cultural context appears in their literary work

response_modes.reason: Without encountering diverse cultural examples, students default to a Western literary norm and treat cultural difference as surface decoration. Multiple cultural contexts — especially First Nations Australian — help students understand how context shapes meaning, not just setting.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cultural context in literature — particularly First Nations Australian literary traditions — is rich territory that goes well beyond pattern recognition into genuine intercultural understanding.
success_criteria: Can explain one way that cultural context shapes how a character or relationship is portrayed in a specific text
Does not treat cultural difference as superficial decoration — can explain how context shapes meaning
